# Models {#sec-models}

To describe trajectories of word learning, we must estimate the number of words children understand, say or sign at different ages. Averages are insufficient: families and practitioners also want to know ranges -- the extents to which children tend to differ at each age. Our target is therefore the distributions of word counts at monthly age intervals, describing both typical counts and the spreads around them.

Previous research, personal experience and evident constraints can inform our expectations. When children are beginning to learn their first words, counts must sit close to zero, so the distribution starts narrow. Children then learn new words at different rates, so as the typical count rises with age, the differences between children compound and the distribution widens. Counts are also bounded -- a child cannot know fewer than zero words, and a checklist cannot record more words than it contains. Vocabulary grows gradually, word by word, so we can expect the distribution to shift and spread smoothly with age rather than to make large jumps over short periods. A statistical model lets us state these expectations precisely and combine them with our data to estimate the distributions we are seeking.

This section introduces our statistical approach -- what statistical models can and cannot claim, and how Bayesian inference expresses uncertainty, uses existing knowledge and supports prediction -- and then describes the models we fit and the assumptions underpinning them.

## Statistical modelling and Bayesian inference

Statistical modelling and inference offer methods for defining mathematical models and fitting them to data to estimate values of interest [@coxPrinciplesStatisticalInference2006; @gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013; @wakefieldBayesianFrequentistRegression2013; @farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018; @spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020; @chanStatisticalModelingComputation2025]. They are central to evaluating scientific theories and interpreting data, and can express what a theory means more precisely than words alone [@farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018, chapter 1].

Statistical models do not by themselves explain how the world works, though they can evaluate the predictions of models that do. A regression model reveals statistical relationships between predictors and outcomes, but those relationships acquire their real-world relevance only within an empirical model -- an account of the real-world phenomenon that informs which statistical and process models can test it [@spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @vanoijenBayesianCompendium2024; @farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018].

The mapping between the two runs both ways: one empirical model admits many statistical models, and one statistical model is consistent with many empirical models. So even when a statistical model fits the observed data well, we cannot be certain its motivating explanation is 'the right one' -- another, equally credible, explanation may fit just as well:

> "Many models correspond to the same hypothesis, and many hypotheses correspond to a single model. This makes strict falsification impossible." [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020, page 4]

Developing and evaluating models is therefore continual and iterative: a competing model may explain the data better, and new observations refine existing models, revise theories and motivate new ones [@gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026].

### Different approaches

There are different approaches to statistical inference, differing in their philosophical and mathematical foundations and in the conclusions they license [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013; @wakefieldBayesianFrequentistRegression2013; @spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026].

Bayesian methods remain uncommon in developmental Down syndrome research, but for the questions this study addresses they offer four notable advantages: (1) probability statements that mean what most people take them to mean; (2) uncertainty expressed as full distributions; (3) a principled way to bring existing knowledge to bear; and (4) direct predictions about individual children [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @bernardoBayesianStatistics2025; @wagenmakersBayesianInferencePsychology2018; @wagenmakersBayesianFrequentistInference2008].

#### Probability as uncertainty

Bayesian inference treats probability as a measure of uncertainty about unknown quantities -- "relative, in part to this ignorance, in part to our knowledge" [@laplaceEssaiPhilosophiqueProbabilites1814] -- so that a number near one marks an event we consider very likely and a number near zero an event we consider very unlikely [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]. On a partly cloudy day, "a 50% chance of rain this afternoon" means that, given what we currently know, rain and no rain seem about equally plausible.

Frequentist uncertainty is instead grounded in how an estimation procedure behaves across repeated samples. A confidence interval is not a probability statement about where the true value lies and does not rank some values as more plausible than others [@moreyFallacyPlacingConfidence2016] -- a distinction that is, unfortunately, often misunderstood [@hoekstraRobustMisinterpretationConfidence2014].

#### Estimates as distributions

Bayesian inference begins with a prior distribution -- what we consider plausible before seeing the data. It then uses Bayes' theorem to update the prior distribution with the data to yield a posterior distribution [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. A Bayesian posterior distribution supports direct and intuitive statements such as: "given our model and the data, the typical 36-month-old child with Down syndrome learns about 5 new words per month, with an 89% probability that the median rate lies between 2 and 7."

#### Using existing knowledge

A prior encodes what is plausible about each parameter before the current data are analysed. Priors can draw on previous research and the experience of people with relevant expertise, where this is available. A well-grounded prior combined with the data yields estimates that are more stable, and often more precise, than the data alone. This can be especially valuable when datasets are small or noisy and a substantial evidence base already exists [@gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020].

The need to specify a prior is sometimes criticised as subjective. However, all statistical analyses rest on subjective assumptions [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024, sec. 5; @bergerStatisticalAnalysisIllusion1988; @benjaminRedefineStatisticalSignificance2017; @stuntWhyWeHabitually2021a]. Arguably, Bayesian priors are more explicit and open to scrutiny. A prior "should be chosen, evaluated, and revised just like all of the other components of the model", and we can test directly how sensitive our estimates are to it [@gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. For this study, priors let us bring existing knowledge of vocabulary development to bear and improve the accuracy of our estimates.

#### Predictions for individual children

From the posterior we can also predict unobserved outcomes. Drawing parameter values from the posterior and simulating a new observation for each draw yields a *posterior predictive distribution* that carries both the randomness in the data and our uncertainty about the parameters [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. This supports statements such as: "given our model and the data, there is an 89% probability that a 36-month-old child with Down syndrome understands between 0 and 142 words" -- a statement that is directly useful for setting expectations about individual children.

#### Computation

Bayesian inference is centuries old [@bayesLIIEssaySolving1763; @LaplaceMemoireProbabilite; @laplaceTheorieAnalytiqueProbabilites1820]. For a while, the calculations required were prohibitive for all but the simplest models. However, this is no longer the case:

> "...this was solved in 1990 through the introduction of Markov chain Monte Carlo to use computational power rather than brute analytical derivation. We now exist in an era where there are no intellectual or analytical impediments to specifying and estimating Bayesian models." [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]

Today, sampling algorithms [@metropolisEquationStateCalculations1953; @hastingsMonteCarloSampling1970; @hoffmanNoUTurnSamplerAdaptively2014] are packaged in freely accessible open-source tools such as Stan and PyMC with interfaces to R and Python [@standevelopmentteamStanLanguageReference2026; @abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023]. Bayesian analysis is consequently now used across economics, political science, ecology, biology, neuroscience, medicine, psychology and education research [@gillBayesianModelingInference2020; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @bonBeingBayesian2020s2023; @pfadtMethodologicalMetamorphosisRapid2025].

## Outcomes {#sec-outcomes}

Vocabulary checklists record a subset of the words a child understands, speaks or signs (@sec-data) at a point in time. Each item is a true or false (checked or not checked) option. A child's score is a count of true responses out of $n$ checklist items. One completion of a checklist (an *administration*) yields up to one count per *outcome* (understood, spoken, signed) for a child of a given age. Each such count (one child, one age, one outcome) is an *observation*. We write $W$ for an observed count, subscripted by outcome where the distinction matters: $W_{\text{und}}$, $W_{\text{spkn}}$ and $W_{\text{sign}}$. Our statistical models must consider how observations are distributed.

### A single reference inventory {#sec-reference-inventory}

Our pooled data include forms with varying numbers of lexical items[^lexical-items] (@sec-data). Checklists are designed to sample the words that children learn earliest, and shorter forms are typically given to younger children. Therefore, for a child with an item count well below a form's maximum, the items a shorter form omits are mostly items that the child does not yet know. Given this, a count recorded on a shorter form will be close to the count a longer checklist would have recorded. We therefore score every count against a single reference inventory of $n = 810$ lexical items, whichever form recorded it, so that every estimate is on the same scale.

[^lexical-items]: Vocabulary checklists contain lexical items presented in a single citation form -- typically the singular form for nouns and the base form for verbs. They do not list all word forms and so cannot count, for example, understanding “pea” and “peas” as understanding two words. 

This approximation is less accurate for children near the maximum of a shorter form, who may know words their form does not ask about but that would have been identified on a longer form. To evaluate the assumption, we examine how often pooled counts approach their form's maximum, test whether raw counts or proportions of each form's maximum better align counts recorded on different checklists, and refit models using only the counts recorded natively on the 810-item checklists.

#### Counts near maxima

Counts near the maximum of a shorter form are uncommon among the data we have pooled for children with Down syndrome: 42 of 977 observations of words understood (4.3%, five of them at the maximum itself) and 18 of 1,428 observations of words spoken (1.3%) fall within 90% of a shorter form's maximum, and none of the 904 observations of words signed do.

The typically developing pool is somewhat more exposed to this the approximation. Among the typically developing studies, every observation comes from a shorter form (@sec-data). Most of these sit well below their form's maximum, because the pool is restricted to ages 8 to 30 months and each form is designed for the ages at which it is given. The exception is spoken vocabulary towards the top of the age range, where typically developing children can approach their form's ceiling. Here, 4.0% of the pool's spoken observations fall within 90% of their form's maximum -- negligible below 22 months, 3.5% at 22 to 25 months, 7.7% at 26 to 27 months, and about one in five observations at 28 to 30 months. Words understood show a similar pattern on a smaller scale: 3.8% overall, rising above 20% only at 23 to 25 months, the oldest ages of the longest-running comprehension form (the 418-item Oxford CDI).

A count at a shorter form's ceiling is effectively censored: the child is credited with every word the form asks about, and under the same easiest-first approximation would have been credited with at least as many -- and plausibly more -- items on the reference inventory. Because the model treats such counts as exact, estimated counts at the oldest typically developing ages are more likely to understate than overstate the count the reference inventory would have recorded. This is a statement about the reference-inventory count, not about spoken vocabulary at large; what checklist counts can and cannot say about vocabulary beyond the words checklists sample is discussed in @sec-data.

#### Forms align more closely on raw counts than on proportions

Two checks provide reassurances for this approximation. First, one study collected parent's observations of 34 children on both the 810-item DSE checklists and the 416-item Oxford CDI (@sec-data). The two forms were not, for the most part, completed together: the Oxford CDI was given at the study's first assessment, and for 24 of the 34 children the DSE checklist is recorded at a different age, up to four months apart and usually later. A measurement model fitted to these dual-form administrations places each form at its own age, links a child's records through a shared child effect, and so estimates the ratio of the two forms' counts at matched age. For words understood it runs from about 0.9 at the youngest dual-form ages to 1.4 by 49 months -- close to the value of 1 that our common scoring assumes over the ages at which shorter forms are typically given -- and it everywhere excludes the 1.95 that rescaling in proportion to form length (810/416) would imply. The estimate does not depend on how the gap between the forms is treated: restricting the model to the ten children whose two forms were recorded at the same age, or assigning every DSE checklist the age at which the child's Oxford CDI was completed, moves the ratio by no more than 0.1 at any age from 25 to 49 months and leaves 1.95 excluded. The rise with age is the compression described above: as the shorter form runs out of items, it records progressively fewer of the words a longer checklist would have identified.

The second reassurance tests the expectation that if shorter forms sampled words in proportion rather than easiest-first, then counts recorded on shorter forms would sit systematically lower. We do not see this in the data: across the typically developing pool, the median counts of words understood align more closely on raw counts than on proportions of each form's maximum at every age from 8 to 15 months, and the shortest form (309 items) does not record the lowest counts.

#### Sensitivity analysis

Finally, we conducted a sensitivity analysis where models were refitted using only the administrations recorded natively on the 810-item DSE checklists, so that no count is scored against a maximum its form did not use. This restriction keeps 278 of the 1,521 administrations in the Down syndrome pool (194 children from four sources, spanning 9 to 115 months), so the restricted fits inform the comparison only where their coverage overlaps the full pool's.

### A Beta-Binomial distribution {#sec-betabinomial}

The words on a checklist are fixed. Therefore, a count $W$ can take only integer values $0 \le W \le n$, and the corresponding proportion $p$ is bounded accordingly. Our outcome model should respect these constraints: counts are discrete, non-negative and bounded above. Since every count in our data is scored against the reference inventory (@sec-reference-inventory), we define $n = 810$.

A count of true responses out of $n$ items follows a Binomial distribution when two assumptions hold within an administration: that (a) given the probability of a true response $p$, the item responses (words checked) are independent; and that (b) every item carries that same probability. This gives a mean of $np$ and a variance (fixed by the mean) of $np(1-p)$ [@gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020, sec. 3.2]. We then assume the same distribution holds across administrations: that (c) the probability is the same for every observation of a given outcome at the same age.

Under the Binomial model, given our inventory of $n = 810$ words, and assuming $p = 0.3$, the expected count would be $np = 243$ with a variance of $np(1-p) = 170.1$ -- a standard deviation of about 13 words. Vocabulary scores vary far more *between* children of the same age than this common probability will allow [@galeoteAcquisitionProductiveVocabulary2008; @marchmanMacArthurBatesCommunicativeDevelopment2023; @zampiniVocabularyDevelopmentChildren2013]. A Beta-Binomial model relaxes assumption (c) by allowing the probability for each observation to vary: rather than one probability shared by all children of an age, each observation's probability is drawn from a Beta distribution [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013, sec. 17.2; @qiaoBetaBinomialModelCount2025].

A Beta-Binomial model also covers departures from assumption (a). Within an administration, responses are unlikely to be truly independent. If one parent completes the whole form, then anything that sways their judgement (for example, a generous or a cautious reading of what counts as "says") sways all the items together. The Beta-Binomial makes no distinction between the two failures: exactly the same distribution of counts arises whether each administration has its own probability or the items within an administration move together, so the two stories cannot be told apart from counts alone. Both are absorbed into the same fitted dispersion.

### The sufficiency of counts

For vocabulary checklists, assumption (b) is false: words differ in difficulty, and some are learned earlier than others. We rely on this ordering to justify our single reference inventory (@sec-reference-inventory), and a hypergeometric test against the three DSE checklists rejects equal item probabilities decisively [**TODO**: ref/appendix]. Nonetheless, under an item-response model in which words differ in difficulty but separate children equally well, the total score carries all the information in the item responses about the child's underlying vocabulary ability [@andersenSufficientStatisticsLatent1977; @fischerDerivationsRaschModel1995]. Two children with the same count are indistinguishable on ability, whichever words make it up, and on a given set of items a higher count always implies a higher estimate of ability. Modelling counts rather than individual words therefore discards nothing about the quantity we care about (for this study). This is a property of the item responses given ability, and the Beta-Binomial leaves it untouched: whatever distribution the probability takes across administrations, the posterior for a child's ability depends on their responses only through the count [@coxPrinciplesStatisticalInference2006, sec. 2.2].

Checklist items will not separate children exactly equally well [@frankVariabilityConsistencyEarly2021, ch. 4; @makranskyItemResponseTheory2016; @kachergisOnlineComputerizedAdaptive2022], so this argument is an approximation. What it costs depends on how far the items depart from equal discrimination, and only item-level responses can show that: the count is sufficient for ability precisely because it discards which words were ticked. Because we model counts, this study cannot measure that cost. The closest comparison we know of suggests the cost is small in practice. Fitting item-response models to the English Words and Sentences data in Wordbank, @frankVariabilityConsistencyEarly2021 [ch. 4] found that a model allowing unequal discrimination fitted better than one that did not, yet no strong evidence that its ability estimates measured children better than measures built from the count. In the two languages with enough repeated administrations to tell, age percentiles of the raw score -- the closest analogue of the age-conditional counts our models describe -- were more stable from one administration to the next than the ability estimates, and they used the sum score for the rest of their analyses.

Moreover, unequal item difficulty makes little difference to the distribution of the count, and the difference it does make runs the opposite way from what one might expect. Consider one child's count on one occasion. Under assumption (b), every word has the same chance of being ticked, so the count behaves like the number of heads in 810 tosses of the same biased coin, and the spread of about 13 words computed above applies. Real words are not like that. For any one child, some words are near-certain to be ticked and others near-certain not to be, and only the words in between are in doubt. A count made up largely of near-certainties is more predictable than a count of coin tosses with the same average, so unequal difficulty narrows the spread of a child's count rather than widening it. (In symbols, the variance of a child's count is the Binomial variance at their average item probability, minus $n$ times the variance of their item probabilities around that average.) At the extreme, a child for whom 243 words are certain and the rest impossible would return exactly 243 every time, where the coin-toss model gives 243 give or take 13.

This narrowing is not small on its own terms, but it matters little for the model, because counts vary for two reasons and this is the smaller one. The first is which of a child's borderline words happen to be ticked on the day; the second is how far children of the same age differ from one another. At every age the second dwarfs the first, as we have seen, so even a large error in the smaller part moves the overall spread by no more than a few per cent, largest at the youngest ages.

[**TODO**: variance shares and worst case; appendix?].

The Beta-Binomial could not show this narrowing in any case: its spread can never fall below the Binomial's, which is its floor. The narrowing is therefore folded into the fitted dispersion along with everything else the count cannot separate. That is one reason we later read the dispersion as a description of how counts are distributed rather than as a measurement of any child (@sec-kappa).

### The limitations of counts

A count loses little of what a checklist has to say about a child's ability, but there are limits to what any count can say. The first is that a count is not a ruler. On a ruler, a centimetre means the same thing wherever it falls; on a checklist, ten words do not. A child's second hundred words may come more easily than the first, or less easily, so equal differences in words need not reflect equal differences in underlying ability (in measurement terms, a count is not an interval scale). The second is that the checklist cannot see below zero words or above the 810 in the reference inventory. Near either end, children who differ a great deal receive nearly the same count: two children with no words yet may be months apart in how close they are to their first, and two children who have exhausted the list may differ by hundreds of words it does not contain.

Ten words gained therefore means different things at different ages and for children at different levels, so change measured in raw words cannot be compared across them. Progress is better read as position relative to peers, but that reading has a limit of its own. A centile is a place in the queue, not a distance along it. It says where a child stands among children of the same age; it does not say how far apart the places are, so a move from the 30th to the 40th centile is neither a fixed number of words nor a fixed amount of growth.

### The outcome model

For the reasons we have discussed in the preceding sections, we therefore model each count as Beta-Binomial with mean proportion $p$ and concentration $\kappa$:

$$
W \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}(n,\,p,\,\kappa),
\qquad
\alpha = p\,\kappa,
\qquad
\beta = (1 - p)\,\kappa,
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the Beta distribution's conventional shape parameters, related to ours by $p = \alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$ and $\kappa = \alpha+\beta$.

Here $p$ is the expected proportion of the checklist that is checked, so the expected count is $\mathrm{E}[W] = np$. The concentration $\kappa$ controls the extra spread (less dispersion): as $\kappa$ grows large the Beta-Binomial approaches the Binomial; as it shrinks, counts spread more widely around the same mean $np$ (more dispersion). This extra variation describes observations around a population trajectory. It should not be confused with uncertainty about the trajectory itself.

Where a model estimates several outcomes jointly (@sec-joint-outcomes), parameters carry the outcome's subscript: $p_{\text{und}}$ is the expected proportion for the count $W_{\text{und}}$, and likewise the concentration $\kappa_{\text{und}}$.

### Age-varying dispersion {#sec-kappa}

For observation $i$ at age $x_i$ months we standardise age,

$$
z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{\sigma_x},
$$

where $\bar{x}$ and $\sigma_x$ are the mean and standard deviation of the ages in the data a model is fitted to, so that $z = 0$ is the average age in that data and one unit of $z$ is $\sigma_x$ months. As a consequence, $z$ means something different in every model, because each is fitted to a different pool of ages: a unit of $z$ spans far fewer months in a model of toddlers than in one spanning childhood. Any prior stated per unit of $z$, such as a slope, therefore expresses a different assumption in months from one model to the next, which is why, wherever we can, we state priors in months (@sec-anchors). Standardising is done to assist computation: the samplers and the Gaussian process approximation (@sec-hsgp) behave better when their inputs are centred near zero and of roughly unit size, and the standardisation itself changes nothing about what a model can express.

Spoken vocabulary counts are more dispersed at older ages than at younger ones [@berglundParentalReportsSpoken2001; @galeoteDevelopmentVocabularySpanish2011; @marchmanMacArthurBatesCommunicativeDevelopment2023; @zampiniLexicalSyntacticDevelopment2011]. We therefore let the conditional dispersion vary smoothly with age:

$$
\kappa(z) = \kappa_{\min} + \exp\!\left(a_\kappa + b_\kappa z\right).
$$

The curve has two parts. The exponential term is the part that changes with age: it rises or falls smoothly, multiplying by the same factor for every $\sigma_x$ months rather than adding the same amount, and it can shrink towards zero but never becomes negative. The constant $\kappa_{\min}$ is the part that does not change, and because the exponential term can never fall below zero, the concentration can never fall below $\kappa_{\min}$ at any age, however young or old. Put together, the curve runs between one level and this floor. For spoken vocabulary, where counts spread out more as children get older, the concentration falls with age towards $\kappa_{\min}$, so the spread of counts grows with age and then levels off rather than growing without limit. The same curve can run the other way, starting at the floor and rising, if the data ask for it.

The priors on this curve changed partway through the family's development. In the earlier form, the priors sit directly on the three quantities in the formula: the floor $\kappa_{\min}$, the intercept $a_\kappa$, and the size of the slope $b_\kappa$, whose sign is fixed so that the concentration can only fall with age. Two of these are hard to picture. $a_\kappa$ sets the age term at the average age of whatever pool the model is fitted to, so its meaning shifts whenever the pool does, and $b_\kappa$ is a rate of change per $\sigma_x$ months, which shifts with it. In the later form, the curve is the same but the priors sit on quantities that can be pictured and checked: the floor, and how far above the floor the curve sits at two named ages, one young and one old. $a_\kappa$ and $b_\kappa$ are then worked out from those, exactly as the mean trend's intercept and slope are worked out from its two reference ages (@sec-anchors). A prior at a named age can be compared with the data at that age, means the same thing whichever pool of ages the model is fitted to, and leaves the direction of the age trend, whether counts spread out or tighten with age, to be decided by the data rather than fixed in advance. Every understood and spoken dispersion curve now uses the later form except in VG05, VG07 and VG08, three development steps that keep the earlier one to remain comparable with the models that descend from them (@sec-model-family); none of the three supplies a reported estimate (@sec-models-of-record), and their dispersion curves are not read as estimates. The signed dispersion curve in VG14 and VG15 also keeps the earlier form, by a separate decision: there the constrained slope is well identified, sits inside its prior and does not press against its constraint, so nothing would be gained by changing it.

## Trends {#sec-trends}

The outcome models (@sec-outcomes) give each observation an expected proportion $p$. To investigate how that proportion changes with age, we model a central (mean) trajectory.

Proportions must lie between zero and one, and relating them to age with a straight line ($p = \beta_0 + \beta_1 z$, say) will eventually stray outside those bounds. We therefore build the trajectory on an unconstrained scale: a predictor $f(z)$ of standardised age (@sec-kappa), free to take any value, transformed by the logistic function,

$$
p(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(f(z)\right) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\left(-f(z)\right)}.
$$

The logistic function returns a value between zero and one whatever the value of $f$. The inverse of this transformation is the *logit*, $\operatorname{logit}(p) = \log\{p/(1-p)\}$.

Vocabulary development may not follow a straight line on the logit scale (perfectly match the S-shaped curve of the logistic function). We therefore give $f$ two parts -- a linear trend, which carries the overall rise with age, and a smooth departure $g$, which captures variations from that trend:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(z) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 z + g(z),\\
g(z) &= \eta\, g_{\mathrm{unit}}(z), \qquad
g_{\mathrm{unit}} \sim \mathcal{GP}\!\left(0,\, k(\cdot,\cdot)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

### Flexible variations from the central trajectory

The straight line carries the overall rise with age. The departure $g$ estimates whatever the straight line misses. We do not know the shape of this departure in advance: it might turn upward sharply in the early years, then flatten, or bend more than once. Rather than preselecting a formula (shape), we describe the kind of curve it might be and then let the data pick from that family. That is what a Gaussian process (GP) does [@rasmussenGaussianProcessesMachine2008; @schulzTutorialGaussianProcess2018]. It is a probability distribution over smooth curves, defined not by a formula but by two rules about behaviour: how smoothly the curve may bend, and how far it may stray.

We can think of this departure as a thin flexible strip laid along the straight line and tethered to it by elastic. The observations act like pins that pull the strip towards them. Between pins the strip bends as little as it can, and where there are no pins for a long stretch it relaxes back to the line. Because many strips are consistent with the same pins, the model works with the whole family of them rather than one: near the pins the family agrees closely, far from them it fans out. The fanning out is the uncertainty about the trajectory. The relaxation to the line is the GP's mean of zero, chosen because the line already carries the rise, so any non-zero mean for $g$ would be indistinguishable from the line itself. Positive $g(z)$ means the population mean at that age sits above the line, and negative $g(z)$ that it sits below.

The length-scale $\ell$ specifies stiffness of the strip. It says over what distance in age the departure at one age still tells you about the departure at another: ages a few months apart must have nearly the same departure, ages far apart are nearly unrelated. A large $\ell$ allows only long slow bends; a small one permits rapid wiggles. The amplitude $\eta$ is the strength of the elastic: it sets how far the strip can typically sit from the line.

In the formulas, the rule of resemblance between ages is the kernel $k(z, z')$. We use the radial basis function (exponentiated-quadratic) kernel with its variance fixed at one,

$$
k(z,z') = \exp\!\left(-\frac{(z-z')^2}{2\ell^2}\right),
\qquad k(z,z) = 1,
$$

and carry the size of the departures in $\eta$ separately, so that $\ell$ alone governs smoothness and $\eta$ alone governs size. The kernel treats all ages alike -- the strip is equally stiff at 36 months and at 72 -- and, given enough data, can follow any smooth trajectory, which suits developmental curves whose precise shape is not known in advance.

#### HSGP approximation {#sec-hsgp}

A Gaussian process is exact but expensive. Describing the strip's shape in full means comparing every observed age with every other, and the cost of that comparison grows with the cube of the number of observations: doubling the data multiplies the work by eight. With several hundred observations per model this would be manageable once, but the sampler must repeat it thousands of times, once for every candidate set of parameter values it tries.

We therefore use the Hilbert-space Gaussian process (HSGP) approximation [@solinHilbertSpaceMethods2020; @riutort-mayolPracticalHilbertSpace2022]. Rather than working with the strip directly, it builds the departure $g_{\mathrm{unit}}$ from a fixed set of smooth waves, from long slow ones to short rapid ones, much as a sound is built from pure tones, and lets the data decide how much of each wave to use. The rules of behaviour are unchanged: the length-scale $\ell$ governs how much of the rapid waves the strip may contain, and the amplitude $\eta$ scales the result exactly as before. The parameters keep their meaning, and the calculation now grows in step with the number of observations rather than with their cube.

Two settings control how faithful the approximation is. The first is the number of waves, $m$. More waves reproduce the strip more closely but cost more to fit, and a strip allowed to bend quickly (a short $\ell$) needs more of them. The second is the width of the age window over which the waves are defined. It must extend some way beyond the ages a model is fitted to, because the approximation deteriorates near its edges, and the boundary factor $c$ sets how far.[^hsgp-domain] Each model confines $\ell$ to a range stated in months, and we choose $m$ and $c$ so that the approximation is accurate across that whole range, following the recommendations implemented in PyMC [@abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023; @riutort-mayolPracticalHilbertSpace2022].

[^hsgp-domain]: The window is centred on the midpoint of the model's declared age domain and extends $c$ times its half-width either side. PyMC's `approx_hsgp_hyperparams` supplies $m$ and $c$ from that domain and the model's length-scale range. Reporting ages are excluded from the domain deliberately, as a presentation choice should not change the fitted model.

### Slope anchors {#sec-anchors}

Rather than placing priors directly on the intercept and slope of the central trajectory ($\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$), we parameterise the linear trend through the expected proportion of words at two reference ages $x_a < x_b$. With $z_a = (x_a - \bar{x})/\sigma_x$ and $z_b = (x_b - \bar{x})/\sigma_x$, and priors placed on $p_{x_a}$ and $p_{x_b}$,

$$
\beta_1 = \frac{\operatorname{logit}(p_{x_b}) - \operatorname{logit}(p_{x_a})}{z_b - z_a},
\qquad
\beta_0 = \operatorname{logit}(p_{x_a}) - \beta_1 z_a .
$$

This gives an interpretable baseline on the logit scale while the GP captures smooth departures.

The reference ages and the priors on $p_{x_a}, p_{x_b}$ are model-specific: 24 and 84 months for the Down syndrome models, 12 and 26 for the typically developing single-outcome models, and 10 and 16 for the young typically developing joint models -- 10 and 21 in VG21, whose age window is wider (@sec-model-family). The priors themselves are Beta distributions on the expected proportion at each reference age, weakly informative and checked by simulating from them before any outcome data are seen (@sec-priorpredictive).

### Summary

@fig-prior-structure illustrates our central trajectory model. It simulates trajectories from our first model's priors before any outcome data are seen. Each faint line is one trajectory the prior considers plausible. The anchor priors say where the straight line is likely to pass at 24 and 84 months, the dotted curve is the trend through the two anchor medians, and one draw is shown twice, before and after the GP, so that the departure is visible as the shaded gap between them.

![Prior trajectories for VG01 (words spoken, Down syndrome), simulated from the model's priors with no outcome data. Faint lines are 250 draws. The bars mark the slope-anchor priors at 24 and 84 months: median, 50% and 89% intervals. The dotted curve is the trend through the anchor medians, S-shaped because the trend is linear on the logit scale. One draw is shown against its own logit-linear trend (dashed) and after the Gaussian-process departure (solid), with the gap between them shaded.](figures/methods/model_structure_prior_vg01){#fig-prior-structure .lightbox}

## Joint outcomes {#sec-joint-outcomes}

The core structure described in the preceding sections is our starting point, used unchanged by our base models with single outcomes: VG01 (words spoken) and VG02 (words understood) for Down syndrome, and VG03 (words spoken) and VG04 (words understood) for typically developing children. The remaining models estimate two or three outcomes jointly. 

### Production nested within understanding

The joint models use the fact that production is logically nested within understanding. They estimate the expected proportion of words understood, $p_{\text{und}}(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(f_{\text{und}}(z)\right)$, together with the *production ratio* -- the expected fraction of understood words that are also spoken:

$$
q(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(h(z)\right),
\qquad
p_{\text{spkn}}(z) = p_{\text{und}}(z)\,q(z),
$$

where $f_{\text{und}}$ and $h$ are logit-scale age predictors, each built as in @sec-trends (a linear trend plus a smooth GP departure): $f_{\text{und}}$ carries the age profile of the proportion understood, and $h$ that of the production ratio. Both factors lie between zero and one, so expected spoken vocabulary can never exceed expected understood vocabulary. Subscripts abbreviate the outcomes throughout: $\text{und}$ for words understood, $\text{spkn}$ for words spoken and, from @sec-signed-words, $\text{sign}$ for words signed.

The nesting also holds count by count, not only in expectation. When an administration records both counts, we model the pair in two steps that mirror how the words relate. The first step models the understood count, out of the full inventory of $n$ items. The second models the spoken count out of the $W_{\text{und}}$ words that child understands -- not out of $n$ -- with $q$ as the expected proportion of them spoken:

$$
\begin{aligned}
W_{\text{und}} &\sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(n,\, p_{\text{und}},\, \kappa_{\text{und}}\right),\\
W_{\text{spkn}} \mid W_{\text{und}} &\sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(W_{\text{und}},\, q,\, \kappa_{\text{spkn}}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the two steps gives a single, coherent probability for the observed pair, and the constraint $0 \le W_{\text{spkn}} \le W_{\text{und}} \le n$ is respected automatically: the model cannot produce a spoken count exceeding the understood count, because the spoken words are drawn from the understood ones. (The rare recorded pairs that violate the constraint are handled separately, below.) $q$ is therefore a genuine conditional proportion for paired, nested counts, not a ratio imposed on marginal means, and each outcome keeps its own age-varying dispersion (@sec-kappa).

@fig-joint-generative shows this structure. Age shapes spoken vocabulary through two routes: by growing the understood vocabulary from which spoken words are drawn, and by changing the fraction of understood words that are spoken.

![The joint model's generative structure. A paired observation's age determines the expected proportion understood and the production ratio; the understood count is drawn from the full inventory, and the spoken count from the child's understood words. Boxes are observed quantities; rounded nodes are latent ones.](diagrams/fig-joint-generative){#fig-joint-generative width="85%"}

This is the model's data-generating graph, not a causal diagram of development. The direction of the factorisation follows the logical nesting of the outcomes -- a child's spoken words are a subset of the words they understand -- and whether comprehension causally enables production is a developmental question these cross-sectional models do not address.

Note also the arrow the diagram does not contain: $q$ varies with age but, given age, not with the size of the child's understood vocabulary -- the understood count affects the spoken count only as the pool of words the ratio applies to. Two same-age children who understand 100 and 400 words are given the same expected production ratio. Whether the ratio additionally depends on comprehension itself is a question we return to with the cross-lag model (VG16, @sec-child-structure).

### The production ratio $q$ {#sec-production-ratio}

The production ratio $q$ is a composition-weighted average, not an item-level probability. Its definition (the fraction of understood words that are also spoken) might invite reading $q$ as the probability that a given word is spoken once understood -- and this would be mistaken. Words differ in difficulty (@sec-betabinomial), and children at a given age understand different numbers of words and different *sets* of words. Therefore, $q$ averages the per-word production probability over whatever vocabulary each contributing child happens to have. Two populations can differ in $q$ purely because their understood vocabularies are composed differently, with no difference in how readily any particular word is produced.[^sufficiency]

[^sufficiency]: The sufficiency argument in @sec-betabinomial is also the proof that this cannot be repaired within a sum-score model: a statistic sufficient for ability carries no information about item composition.

It should also be noted that a contrast at matched comprehension is not a contrast at matched age. Where the report compares Down syndrome and typically-developing children at the same level of comprehension, the two groups are 8–13 months apart in age at that matched level. A difference in $q$ read off such a comparison is therefore a difference between groups that are simultaneously unlike in age and in vocabulary composition, and neither can be held fixed while varying the other. Both qualifications apply wherever $q$ is reported.

### Levelling the production ratio's trend above its high anchor {#sec-clamp}

The Down syndrome joint models are evaluated from 8 to 115 months, but their anchors sit at 24 and 84, so about a quarter of that range lies above the high anchor, where the linear trend is extrapolating. The trend is a straight line on the logit scale, and a line steep enough to climb between the anchors keeps climbing beyond them, which the logistic transformation turns into an approach to 1. For a vocabulary proportion out of 810 words this is harmless, because even at 115 months the proportion stays well short of the ceiling. For the production ratio it is not: the ratio genuinely approaches 1, so its logit saturates.[^vg10_extrapolation]

[^vg10_extrapolation]: Extrapolated to 115 months, VG10's fitted trend alone put the ratio at 0.99, and did so with 90% probability across the posterior, against 0.84 once the GP's correction is included. Only a handful of administrations record both counts above 78 months, so nothing in the data supports the claim, and the GP was spending most of its amplitude hauling the trajectory back where there are no data while sitting almost idle at 48 months where there are.

We therefore level the production ratio's trend off above the high anchor. In the linear term, $z$ is replaced by a smoothed version of $\min(z, z_b)$,

$$
z_{\text{eff}} = z_b - \frac{1}{s}\operatorname{softplus}\!\big(s\,(z_b - z)\big),
\qquad s = \frac{50}{z_b - z_a},
$$

so the trend rises as before up to $z_b$ and is flat beyond it.[^clamp-sharpness] The GP is not levelled. It remains free to carry departures above the anchor, but it is projected in the same levelled coordinate (@sec-gpanchor), so that it cannot reintroduce the slope the levelling removed.

[^clamp-sharpness]: The sharpness $s$ is set from the anchor span, so the rounding of the corner is the same fraction of the span in every model: the largest difference from a hard minimum is $\beta_1 \log 2 / s$, or 1.4% of the span, about 0.8 months of age for the Down syndrome models. A hard minimum was tried first. Its derivative jumps at the anchor, and the fitted spoken trajectory inherited a visible elbow and briefly fell with age.

This clamp is one-sided. Below the low anchor the line extrapolates well (VG10's ratio at 12 months is 0.019 by extrapolation against 0.022 fitted), and levelling there would instead pin young ages at the 24-month value. In addition, it applies to the production ratio only. The understood trend never approaches its ceiling in any posterior draw, and the single-outcome models on the same pool and anchors show no runaway.[^levelling-both]

[^levelling-both]: Levelling both trends was also actively harmful: expected spoken vocabulary is the product $p_{\text{und}}\,q$, and two levelled factors multiplied together put a corner in the spoken trajectory at exactly 84 months, an anchor choice masquerading as a developmental event. Restricting the levelling to $q$ removed the corner and moved nothing below 72 months by more than 0.7%.

The cost of this clamp is small. The high anchor's prior no longer describes exactly the trend at 84 months but a value short of it by that same 1.4% of the span; between the anchors the trend is untouched, so both anchor priors carry over unchanged.

Moving the high anchor upward instead was considered and rejected: the anchor is shared by the understood and production-ratio trends, and above 84 months comprehension is observed on only 13 administrations from 12 children, too few to place a prior on, while the high anchor already lies beyond the ages at which comprehension is reported [**TODO**: section cross-ref].

The levelling applies to the production ratio in every Down syndrome joint and signing model: VG05, VG07–VG10 and VG14–VG16 directly, and VG19, VG20 and VG22 through the VG10 definition they derive from. The signed ratio @sec-signed-words needs none, because its three-anchor trend levels off beyond its oldest reference age by construction. The typically developing models do not level, because their evaluation ranges extend barely beyond their high anchors. The single-outcome Down syndrome baselines, VG01 and VG02, extrapolate the line across the full range, for the reason given above.

### Signed words {#sec-signed-words}

The signing models add a third outcome and treat it as they treat speech: a signed word is one of the words the child understands. Alongside the production ratio they estimate a *sign ratio* $r$, the expected fraction of understood words that the child also signs,

$$
r(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(f_{\text{sign}}(z)\right),
\qquad
p_{\text{sign}}(z) = p_{\text{und}}(z)\,r(z),
$$

and score a signed count against the child's understood count, exactly as the spoken count is scored:

$$
W_{\text{sign}} \mid W_{\text{und}} \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(W_{\text{und}},\, r,\, \kappa_{\text{sign}}\right).
$$

Signed vocabulary can therefore never exceed understood vocabulary, and $r$ carries the same qualifications as $q$: it averages over whatever words each child happens to understand, and is not the probability that any particular word is signed (@sec-production-ratio). Signing is recorded only in the Down syndrome sources; one of them defines its column to include spontaneous symbolic gestures alongside taught signs (@sec-data).

@fig-signing-generative extends @fig-joint-generative with the third outcome: the signed count is drawn from the child's understood words exactly as the spoken count is, each through its own ratio.

![The signing models' generative structure. Age determines the expected proportion understood, the production ratio and the sign ratio; the understood count is drawn from the full inventory, and the spoken and signed counts are each drawn from the child's understood words. Boxes are observed quantities; rounded nodes are latent ones.](diagrams/fig-signing-generative){#fig-signing-generative width="85%"}

Signing follows a different course from speech. It typically emerges early, peaks in the preschool years and then declines as spoken words take over [@kaat-vandenosExpressiveVocabularyDevelopment2017], so a trend that only rises cannot describe it. Nor can the GP be left to supply the shape on its own. Its prior is centred on zero departure at every age, so with a flat trend the prior would say that signing is equally common at every age, and the data would have to build the whole hill unaided. $f_{\text{sign}}$ therefore replaces the single straight line with a *tent*: priors on the ratio at three reference ages, 15, 36 and 96 months, joined by straight lines on the logit scale, so that the trend rises to the middle reference age and falls after it, and is flat beyond the outer two. The GP adds smooth departures as before. In VG14 the peak sits at 36 months by construction, so its height is estimated but its age is asserted. VG15, the model of record, gives the peak's position between the outer reference ages a prior and estimates it, so the age at which signing peaks is a finding rather than an assumption.

As with the other trends, the GP is stripped of anything the tent itself could express (@sec-gpanchor), so the three reference levels keep their meaning. Even so, the signed trajectory leans on its parametric shape more heavily than the other outcomes lean on theirs. Signed observations are dense from about 12 to 60 months and thin beyond, the outer reference ages are asserted rather than fitted, and the GP's length-scale is only weakly identified, so at older ages the curve is shaped more by the prior than by the data. Whether signing and speaking cluster on the same words is a separate question, taken up next (@sec-speech-sign-association).

### The sign--speech association {#sec-speech-sign-association}

Our first model to include signing (VG14) treats speaking and signing as conditionally independent given understanding: among the words a child understands at a given age, whether one is signed says nothing about whether it is also spoken. Independence is a deliberately simple starting point, and its weight falls on a derived quantity of real practical interest -- total expressive vocabulary, the words a child says *or* signs -- which under independence is computed from the two ratios rather than estimated from evidence about their overlap.

VG15 estimates the association instead, because four pooled sources record production word by word in both modalities and so carry more than marginal counts. uk_02 and uk_07 record, for each understood word, whether the child signs it, says it, does both or neither; es_01 records totals from which the same four cells follow by subtraction -- with the caveat that its non-vocal column is defined to include spontaneous symbolic gestures alongside taught signs, and may cover only ten of its form's 21 word categories (@sec-data); and nz_01 records, within produced words, whether each is spoken, signed or both. These compositions are scored with a Dirichlet-Multinomial term in place of the separate spoken and signed likelihood contributions -- each composition is conditional on its observed total, so the understood likelihood is unchanged -- and the association is carried by a Plackett odds ratio $\psi$: among the words a child understands, the factor by which being signed multiplies the odds of also being spoken. $\psi = 1$ recovers VG14's independence; $\psi > 1$ means signing and speaking cluster on the same words.

@fig-sign-speech-composition shows how this changes the structure of @fig-signing-generative. Among the words a child understands, each is neither spoken nor signed, spoken only, signed only, or both. The composition is observed for the four word-level sources and latent elsewhere, where only its margins, the spoken and signed counts, enter the likelihood; $\psi$ couples the two modalities within it. Removing $\psi$ gives VG14, in which the margins reduce to the two conditional likelihoods above.

![How VG15 scores production in both modalities. Among the words a child understands, each is neither spoken nor signed, spoken only, signed only, or both. The composition (dashed) is observed for the four sources that record production word by word and latent elsewhere, where only its margins enter. The association $\psi$ (dashed) couples the two modalities within understood words; removing it gives VG14, in which the margins reduce to the two conditional likelihoods. Boxes are observed quantities; rounded nodes are latent ones.](diagrams/fig-sign-speech-composition){#fig-sign-speech-composition width="85%"}

$\psi$ carries a study-level random term, because the informing sources disagree by more than sampling error and the disagreement is not an age effect in disguise: fitted without a study term an age trend looks strong, but age alone fits the cross-tabulations worse than study alone and adds nothing once study is included, and sources matched on age still differ severalfold. With only four informing sources the between-study spread is itself weakly identified and the prior does real work, so the per-study values, not the pooled centre, are the primary read wherever $\psi$ is reported. Which sources' signing fields measure total signed vocabulary -- and which are masked, or reintroduced only as sensitivity analyses -- is a data question, addressed in @sec-data.

### When only one count of a pair is recorded

When the understood count is unavailable, the spoken or signed count remains usable through a marginal fallback,

$$
W_{\text{spkn}} \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(n,\, p_{\text{und}}\,q,\, \kappa_{\text{spkn}}\right),
$$

and analogously for signing. A recorded spoken or signed count greater than its understood count is retained through the same fallback and counted as a source-data violation in the fit log rather than silently discarded.

The fallback reuses the conditional branch's dispersion $\kappa_{\text{spkn}}$, and that is an approximation: on conditional rows the dispersion is variation in $q$ alone, whereas fallback rows also absorb unobserved variation in $p_{\text{und}}$. The size of the approximation is bounded exactly: the true marginal of a fallback row is more dispersed than the fallback's Beta-Binomial precisely when $q\,\kappa_{\text{spkn}} > \kappa_{\text{und}}$ -- the level $p_{\text{und}}$ drops out entirely -- and the two variances are equal on the boundary.[^fallback-moments] The fallback is therefore neither conservative nor anti-conservative as a structural matter: which way a given model errs is a question about its fitted concentrations. Three registered sensitivity analyses bound it in practice -- dropping the fallback rows altogether, giving the fallback branch its own dispersion through a single signed scalar that nests the default at zero, and replacing the fallback's dispersion with the one matching the true marginal's first two moments -- and posterior-predictive calibration is reported separately for the conditional and fallback rows, which differ systematically in age and study composition.

[^fallback-moments]: Binomial thinning collapses the paired factorisation to $W_{\text{spkn}} \mid \theta_{\text{und}}, \theta_{\text{spkn}} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}\!\left(n,\, \theta_{\text{und}}\theta_{\text{spkn}}\right)$, so the true marginal of a fallback row is a Binomial mixed over the *product* of two independent Beta variates. That product is not itself Beta, but both its moments are elementary, and comparing them with the fallback's reduces to the single condition given here.

## Multilevel models {#sec-randomeffects}

To separate the population age curves from differences in study composition and from repeated measurements on the same child, we add random intercepts on the logit-scale predictors at the observation level. For a predictor $f_\bullet \in \{f_{\text{und}}, h, f_{\text{sign}}\}$,

$$
f_\bullet(z_i) \;\to\; f_\bullet(z_i) + \delta^{\text{study}}_{\bullet,\,s(i)} + \delta^{\text{subj}}_{\bullet,\,j(i)},
\qquad
\delta_\bullet \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \tau_\bullet),\ \ \tau^{\text{study}}_\bullet \sim \mathrm{HalfNormal}(0.5),\ \ \tau^{\text{subj}}_\bullet \sim \mathrm{HalfNormal}(1.5),
$$

implemented non-centred, where $s(i)$ and $j(i)$ index the study and subject of observation $i$. The two levels take different scales because they are on different scales in the data: fitting the same grouping structure outside the models puts the between-child standard deviation at 0.74–1.15 on the logit scale across the family, where between-study differences are around a third of that. Study intercepts absorb between-lab/between-study level differences; subject intercepts stop within-child repeated measurements being treated as independent. **The reported population curves set every random effect to zero**, so their interpretation is unchanged. Tiny studies can be trimmed before fitting (`min_study_observations`) to avoid near-unidentified intercepts.

The TD hierarchical models apply the same repeated-measures rule. VG11 and VG12 include a child intercept on their single outcome, and VG13 includes child intercepts on both $p_{\text{und}}$ and $q$. A fixed-seed sensitivity retains one randomly selected administration per study-specific child and disables the child effects, providing a cheaper check that conclusions do not depend on treating repeat administrations as additional independent children.

### Anchoring the smooth departure {#sec-gpanchor}

Random intercepts introduce a redundancy the single-level models do not have. The trajectory's level can now be written three ways -- in the linear trend, in a constant drift of the GP, or in the intercepts -- and different combinations of the three produce identical fitted curves. The data cannot prefer a point along such a ridge, so the sampler wanders it, and in the models with subject effects on both trajectories this degraded sampling badly: strong posterior correlations between the trend and the GP's amplitude and length-scale, and the family's worst convergence diagnostics in the models that lacked the fix.

The fix pins the GP. In the anchored models the smooth departure $g$ is, in every posterior draw, exactly zero at a reference age, always the midpoint of the model's two anchor ages -- 54 months for the anchored Down syndrome models, 19 for VG11 and VG12, 13 for VG13 and VG23, and 15.5 for VG21 -- and $g$ is additionally stripped of any component across the observed ages that the trend itself could express, computed from the observed rows only so that reporting grids cannot influence the likelihood. The trend then owns level and slope, the intercepts own group shifts, and the GP owns only curvature. This changes how a given curve is written, not which curves the model can express, and where the production ratio's trend is levelled above its high anchor the projection uses the same levelled coordinate, so the two devices stay consistent (@sec-clamp). VG10 is exactly VG09 plus this device, introduced when subject effects on the production ratio surfaced the ridge; VG15, VG16 and the hierarchical typically developing models carry it for the same reason, and every later model inherits it from VG10 or VG13. The earlier development steps (VG05, VG07–VG09, VG14) predate it.

## Child-level structure {#sec-child-structure}

A random intercept gives each child one constant offset per trajectory: children may differ in level, but every child's curve is parallel to the population's on the logit scale, and a child's standing on one outcome says nothing about their standing on another. Neither restriction is innocent, and four registered models relax them in different directions. Three are parallel refinements of VG10 -- alternatives, not a sequence -- and each contains its parent as a special case, so in every case the data are free to answer 'no change'. The fourth extends VG09 with a predictor rather than a random effect, and asks a different kind of question.

### Correlated child effects

VG10 draws each child's two offsets -- on understanding, and on the production ratio -- independently. That is an assumption, and a testable one: are children who understand more for their age also more, or less, likely to say what they understand? **VG20** frees exactly one parameter, the correlation $\rho_{uq}$ between the two offsets, under a prior (LKJ with $\eta = 2$) that pulls gently toward zero so that a correlation must be evidenced rather than assumed. VG10 is nested exactly at $\rho_{uq} = 0$; the built model differs by that parameter and nothing else. Because the correlation acts at the child level, the population trajectories are essentially unmoved; what it changes is prediction for individual children, whose two effects now move together rather than independently.

**VG23** adds the same block, under the same prior, to the young typically developing joint model (VG13), so the two populations' correlations are estimated comparably. Its registration reason is identification as much as substance. The typically developing pool averages barely more than one administration per child, so separating stable between-child differences from occasion-to-occasion variation rests almost entirely on the likelihood's functional form; but every administration yields two counts from the same child on the same day, and their agreement informs the child effect on every row rather than only on the minority with a repeat visit. The catch is stated at registration rather than discovered later: both counts come from one questionnaire completed by one parent, so a shared reporter tendency is indistinguishable from shared child ability and biases the correlation upward, where the variance-partition route biases the same quantity downward -- the two designs bracket the truth rather than resolving it.

### Child slopes

Level and rate are different facts, and a constant offset conflates them: it cannot express a child who is behind but moving quickly, or ahead but slowing. **VG19** gives each child a rate as well as a level on both trajectories. The child's shift at age $a$ becomes $b_0 + b_1 (a - 36)/12$: the level $b_0$ is defined at 36 months (the pool's median age, which stops level and rate trading off in the sampler), the rate $b_1$ is per year, and each outcome's level and rate are drawn jointly with an estimated correlation. VG10 is nested exactly at zero rate spread, and the level keeps VG10's own prior, so the extension is one-factor. The structure was chosen on fitted residuals before any of it was implemented: a random slope beat a constant intercept decisively on the spoken outcome ($2\,\Delta\log L = 36.1$, and 20.8 when restricted to the 334 children with repeated spoken measures), while an autoregressive alternative collapsed to zero persistence -- the missing structure is persistent drift, not occasion-to-occasion wobble. Both outcomes carry a slope because the likelihood sees only their product on spoken rows, so the evidence cannot say which outcome owns the drift.

VG19 and VG20 are deliberately not combined. VG20 correlates the two outcomes' levels; VG19 correlates each outcome's own level with its own rate. Their union is a four-by-four covariance whose most interesting element -- do children who gain comprehension faster also convert it to speech faster? -- is estimated by neither, and bolting the two together would assume it away. Asking that question properly is VG22's job.

### A low-rank factor

**VG22** holds all four child effects -- level and rate on understanding, level and rate on the production ratio -- in one structure: $b = Lz$, with $z$ a $k$-dimensional standard normal deviate per child and $L$ a $4 \times k$ loading matrix, so the implied covariance is positive semi-definite by construction. A free four-by-four covariance was examined first and rejected by the data themselves: its maximum-likelihood correlation matrix is singular, a rank-3 factor reaches the identical likelihood, and the rate-to-rate coupling that motivated the idea is the weakest of the six cross-terms. The number of dimensions ('rank') is therefore declared in the definition rather than inferred -- the residual likelihood cannot separate ranks 2 and 3 and carries almost no information about a fourth -- and ranks 1 to 3 are fitted as a registered sensitivity family. Rank 1 asserts perfect correlation among all four effects by construction, and fails in exactly that way, which is itself informative. The marginal scales keep the names, priors and meanings they carry in VG19 and VG20, and the level-level correlation $\rho_{uq}$ is given the same LKJ-form prior VG20 places on it -- designed into the loading geometry rather than left to whatever distribution that geometry would otherwise induce -- so the two models estimate the shared quantity under the same prior and a difference between them cannot be a prior artefact.

### The cross-lag

The joint models make the production ratio a function of age alone: given age, a child's understood vocabulary affects their expected spoken count only as the pool the ratio applies to (@sec-joint-outcomes). **VG16** asks whether comprehension history shifts the ratio itself. For children observed more than once, the previous administration's understood count -- expressed as a residual against the population curve, and assigned per complete administration wave so the construction cannot depend on the order rows happen to arrive in -- enters the current production ratio with a coefficient $\beta_{\text{lag}}$, under a prior centred on zero so that neither direction is imposed. The estimand needs careful reading: because a population-relative predictor retains each child's persistent standing, $\beta_{\text{lag}}$ is a history-conditioned mixture of between-child and within-child association, not an isolated within-child dynamic and not evidence of temporal direction. VG16 exists to estimate this single quantity and supplies no other reported number; its numerical estimate is currently withdrawn while a corrected lag construction awaits a reporting-quality refit (@sec-models-of-record).

## The model family {#sec-model-family}

Twenty models are registered. They are numbered in roughly the order they were developed -- a higher number means 'added later', not 'better' -- and they differ along three axes: population, outcome(s), and which of the components described above they carry. Development was deliberately incremental, one named piece of structure at a time, so the family records its own history, and most members exist to show what a single assumption contributes rather than to supply reported numbers (@sec-models-of-record). @tbl-model-family lists them all.

| Model | Population           | Outcomes                     | Structure and purpose                                                                                                                                                 |
| ----- | -------------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
