: The registered models. {#tbl-model-family}

The gaps in the numbering are deliberate. VG06, the original typically developing joint model, was retired outright when the instrument supplying most of its comprehension rows proved to record comprehension as a proxy for production; VG13 replaced rather than repaired it. VG17 and VG18 are reserved for exploratory, unregistered prototypes that bypass the validation machinery below (@sec-estimation); their output is not validatable and none of it is published.

The main Down syndrome lineage runs VG05 → VG07 → VG08 → VG09 → VG10, adding one level of hierarchy at a time, with VG19, VG20 and VG22 as parallel refinements of VG10's child structure and VG16 as a single-purpose offshoot of VG09. The signing lineage runs VG14 → VG15. On the typically developing side, VG11 and VG12 are the single-outcome reference models, and VG13 -- with VG21 and VG23 derived from it -- the joint one. For the full statistical detail of any single model -- its priors, prior predictive evidence, diagnostics, sensitivity variants and findings -- see its technical report, published alongside this one; this chapter carries the shared machinery and what each model adds.

## Estimation and validation {#sec-estimation}

### The iterative workflow

We follow the iterative Bayesian workflow described by @gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020: specify a transparent model, simulate from its priors, fit it, inspect computation and predictive behaviour, identify a concrete inadequacy, and only then add structure. The numbered models preserve that development history. A later number is not automatically better: an extension must solve a named problem and survive the same checks as its predecessor, and @sec-models-of-record records which models currently carry reported numbers.

### The fitting pipeline

Models are defined in PyMC and sampled with the NUTS sampler [@abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023; @hoffmanNoUTurnSamplerAdaptively2014]. Every registered model runs the same ordered pipeline: prepare data; construct priors; build the model; prior predictive checks; sampling; convergence diagnostics; posterior predictive checks; posterior summaries, plots and the model report. Three sampling configurations exist -- a short development configuration, an intermediate testing one, and a reporting-quality one -- and only reporting-quality fits can source a numerical claim in this report. Each fit is written to an isolated staging area and promoted atomically only after the statistical pipeline succeeds, so a failed or interrupted run can never overwrite a good fit, and report rendering runs afterwards as a separate, retryable step.

### Prior predictive checks {#sec-priorpredictive}

Before the models see the study outcomes, we draw trajectories and replicated scores from the priors alone. We require bounded scores, plausible levels at the youngest and oldest relevant ages, developmental change that is smooth on a realistic time scale, and enough dispersion to represent heterogeneous children without placing substantial probability on implausible extremes. A prior predictive failure is addressed by revising the assumptions or their parameterisation -- never by inspecting the posterior and selecting a prior that reproduces it.

### Convergence diagnostics {#sec-convergence}

Every reported fit is screened against four diagnostics, in two tiers. The **hard tier** fails closed: a potential scale reduction factor $\hat{R} \le 1.01$ and bulk and tail effective sample sizes of at least 400 on every sampled parameter, vector-valued parameters included [@vehtariRankNormalizationFolding2021]. A fit that misses either is not summarised, rendered or published at all, because a chain that has not mixed cannot be summarised. The **soft tier** -- no divergent transitions, and an energy BFMI of at least 0.3 on every chain -- is recorded rather than fail-closed: both diagnostics bear on how well the sampler reached the posterior's tails, so they qualify interval bounds more than point estimates, and a fit carrying a soft-tier caveat may be published only with the caveat attached wherever its numbers are read. Bulk and tail effective sample sizes are gated separately because they govern different summaries: bulk bounds the Monte Carlo error of the medians we tabulate, tail that of the interval limits we lead with (@sec-interval-convention).

### Posterior predictive checks and calibration {#sec-predictive-calibration}

Posterior predictive checks generate replicated outcomes from the fitted model and compare them with the observations: distributional overlays, bounded-count behaviour across age and, for the joint models, the paired outcomes together, fallback rows included; the signing model additionally checks the sign-by-speech cells that identify $\psi$. Alongside the visual checks, every fit writes a numerical calibration table recording, for each outcome, overall and within age bands, the mean observed and predicted counts, the empirical coverage of the predictive interval at its stated width, and the distribution of the probability integral transform -- each observation's position within its own predictive distribution. Coverage near nominal and a near-uniform transform indicate a predictive distribution that is neither too wide nor overconfident, and departures are directional, so the table says not only whether but how a model misfits. These checks are in-sample -- the replications condition on parameters the same observations informed -- so their value is comparative, across models, outcomes and ages, and gross misfit is what they catch first; the out-of-sample counterpart is the comparison standard below (@sec-supersedes). A model can pass every sampler diagnostic and fail these checks: convergence shows that computation characterised the specified posterior, not that the specification represents the data.

### Parameter recovery

For the models that carry reported numbers, we simulate data from the model at known parameter values, refit the model to the simulation with the same pipeline, and score the recovered posterior against the truth. A replicate counts only if its own fit converges. A handful of replicates can expose a parameter the design cannot recover, or intervals that miss their nominal coverage badly; it cannot certify fine calibration, and it is read accordingly.

### Sensitivity analyses

Where a defensible alternative exists to a data rule, a prior or a structural choice, it is registered as a named variant and fitted with the same pipeline rather than argued about: each masked data-defect class has a reinstatement variant, the priors that carry real weight have widened counterparts, the young typically developing window has alternative widths, and the fallback likelihood has three registered alternatives (@sec-joint-outcomes). A variant's fit is compared with the baseline quantity by quantity against the baseline's own posterior intervals, so a robustness claim in this report is a measurement, not an impression.

### Model comparison, and what 'supersedes' means {#sec-supersedes}

A later model supersedes an earlier one only on two grounds together: a tabulated out-of-sample comparison -- leave-one-out expected log predictive density, with the standard error of the difference, so the improvement is quantified rather than asserted -- and an identified structural issue in the earlier model that the later one resolves. Four statuses follow: a **model of record** is the current source for a stated estimand; a **development step** is retained to show how structure was added but supplies no headline number; a **reference** model is a typically developing comparison with a distinct population role; and a **superseded** model has been replaced after a documented structural or data problem. A superseded model never supplies a number in the findings.

### Reporting conventions {#sec-interval-convention}

For every parameter and derived quantity we report the posterior median, an inner 50% and an outer 89% credible interval, and -- through the density and predictive plots -- the full posterior rather than an interval alone [@kruschkeBayesianAnalysisReporting2021]. Intervals are equal-tailed by default; a small named set of strongly skewed or boundary-censored estimands -- the sign--speech association $\psi$, the concentration $\kappa$, and milestone and peak ages -- is reported with highest-density intervals instead, and each table and figure states which kind it uses. The width is 89% rather than the familiar 95% deliberately: no width carries special epistemic status, a non-round one discourages reading an interval as a significance test [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020], and the 5.5th and 94.5th percentile limits of an 89% interval are almost exactly what the tail diagnostic in @sec-convergence certifies, where a 95% interval's more extreme limits are harder to estimate at the same effective sample size. Because the full posterior is reported, a reader who prefers another width can take it directly.

Several estimands rest on modest samples, and a point estimate selected for looking decisive is on average inflated in magnitude and can even take the wrong sign -- the Type-M and Type-S errors that follow from selecting on a noisy estimate. We therefore lead with the interval and the strength of evidence for a named claim, and treat the point estimate as the least informative summary.

Two kinds of uncertainty band appear in the findings, and their scopes differ. **Population-trajectory intervals** carry posterior uncertainty about the typical child's curve in an average study -- every random effect set to zero -- and narrow as data accrue; they say nothing about how far individual children spread. **New-child predictive intervals** additionally draw a fresh child from the estimated between-child variation (holding the study effect at zero), and are the ones to quote when setting expectations for an individual child. Milestone-age summaries likewise describe the population trajectory's crossing age, not the spread of individual children's milestone ages. Which kind a number is, is stated wherever it is reported.

### Provenance

Every fit records a manifest carrying the complete model definition, the sampling configuration, fingerprints of the raw inputs, an exact hash of the prepared analysis data, and the code revision and environment that produced it. Before any figure or table reaches this report, the fit behind it is re-validated field by field against the current definitions and data rules, so a posterior that predates a change to either is identified as stale and cannot be republished silently. The same checks gate the model-comparison outputs, and each model's technical report carries its per-fit diagnostic record.

## Models of record {#sec-models-of-record}

Which model supplies each reported estimate is a recorded decision under the taxonomy of @sec-supersedes, reviewed whenever a model is added or a defect is found -- never an implication of the numbering. Between them, the current assignments cover the study's aims (@sec-intro): the Down syndrome trajectories, ranges and milestone summaries, and the contrasts with typically developing children.

### Words understood

The Down syndrome comprehension estimates come from **VG20**, the joint model of record. It replaced VG10 in August 2026, when VG10's assumption of independent child effects was contradicted by its own fitted deviations; the population trajectories are reproduced essentially unchanged, so the succession supersedes VG10's child-level intervals rather than withdrawing its curves. Down syndrome comprehension quantities are reported to 72 months: the 72–84-month band is populated, but the candidate child structures disagree there by most of an interval width while remaining indistinguishable out of sample, so a number in that band would reflect the model choice more than the data. The typically developing comprehension reference is **VG12**, reported to 25 months, where its pool's comprehension observations stop.

### Words spoken

The Down syndrome spoken estimates likewise come from **VG20**, whose spoken trajectory is the product of its understood trajectory and production ratio; spoken quantities are reported to 90 months. The typically developing spoken reference is **VG11**. For the comparison of the two populations at matched comprehension, the joint typically developing model of record is **VG13**; the study owner has adopted the wider 8–22-month window for that comparison, and its registered successor **VG21** takes the role once it has a reporting-quality fit that passes the checks above.

### Words signed or gestured

The signing estimates -- the signed trajectory $r(a)$, the sign--speech association $\psi$ and total expressive vocabulary -- come from **VG15**. **VG14** is its development step, retained because the pair measures exactly what the independence assumption would have cost.

### The rest of the family

VG05, VG07, VG08, VG09, VG10 and VG14 are development steps and supply no reported numbers; the single-outcome baselines VG01–VG04 serve as unclamped, single-level controls on the machinery. VG16's single estimand -- the comprehension-history cross-lag -- is withdrawn until its corrected construction passes a reporting-quality fit. VG19, VG22 and VG23 are registered refinements whose reporting roles have not yet been assigned, and VG21 and VG23 are not yet fitted. When an assignment changes, this section and the affected models' technical reports change with it.
